analysis.one_liner: Forces banking regulators to scrap proposed rules requiring the largest banks to hold more capital against losses.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 3 House Republicans with no Democratic support, never received a committee hearing or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In September 2023, the three federal bank regulators proposed tighter capital rules for the largest U.S. banks, requiring them to hold a bigger financial cushion against potential losses instead of relying mostly on their own internal risk models. This bill would force the regulators to withdraw that proposal and permanently bar them from issuing any 'substantially similar' rule. It was introduced by one House Republican with two cosponsors and died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the largest banks — especially those with big trading operations — would have avoided the proposed requirement to hold more capital against potential losses. That would have protected their profits and preserved their ability to pay dividends and buy back their own stock at current levels.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require the OCC, the Federal Reserve, and the FDIC to withdraw their proposed capital rule for large banking organizations, releasing those banks from the proposed stricter requirements [S2, S3].

It goes further than a simple delay: it would prohibit the agencies from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing the proposed rule 'or any substantially similar rule,' permanently blocking this approach to bank capital regulation [S3].
Banks would keep using their own internal credit risk models rather than the standardized approach aligned with international Basel standards that the rule would have required [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers would bear more of the risk. Lower capital cushions mean that when a big bank suffers large losses, more of the damage lands on the FDIC's deposit insurance fund — which is ultimately backstopped by taxpayers — and on creditors and customers, rather than being absorbed by the bank's own resources first.
analysis.who_pays_short: Depositors, the FDIC fund, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Blocking the rule would leave the largest banks with thinner loss-absorbing cushions, increasing the chance that a shock at one of them becomes a taxpayer-backed rescue, as recent bank failures showed [S2].
The bill would permanently bar 'substantially similar' rules by statute, taking away the regulators' ability to revisit the issue even if future events showed more capital was needed [S3].

The strongest good-faith objection to the underlying rule — that it could raise banks' costs, constrain lending, and push some risk-taking into less-regulated nonbank lenders — is a real debate; this bill sidesteps it entirely by removing the rule rather than revising it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs to the public outweigh the benefits to the industry. Banks have legitimate arguments about how the rule was calibrated, but this bill does not refine it — it abolishes it and locks the door against any similar rule by statute, leaving the biggest banks with the same light-touch capital treatment that preceded recent bank failures. The public pays for that risk through deposit insurance exposure and bailout backstops.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Andrew Ogles introduced the Stop Basel Endgame Act on January 30, 2024, joined by Rep. Byron Donalds, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1, S3, S5].
It attracted 2 cosponsors, both Republicans out of 224 House Republicans [S4].
The only action ever taken was the committee referral; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest banks gained nothing they did not already have, but they also avoided a floor vote on record. Because the bill died, the banking agencies kept their legal authority to finalize stricter capital rules for the biggest banks, and depositors and taxpayers were spared a statutory prohibition on that safeguard. The industry's allies avoided any recorded vote on whether big banks should hold more capital.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Regulators kept authority; banks avoided a recorded vote

for.name: Rep. Andrew Ogles
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to force regulators to withdraw the proposed large-bank capital rule

for.name: Rep. Byron Donalds
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as an original cosponsor

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services (Chair Patrick McHenry, R)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it

sides.party_line_note: All sponsorship was Republican: Rep. Ogles plus 2 of 224 House Republicans as cosponsors, with no Democratic cosponsors, and the bill never advanced [S4].

industries.industry: Large banks with significant trading activity (banks over roughly $100 billion in assets)
industries.note: The proposed rule would require these banks to hold more capital against potential losses and replace internal risk models with a standardized approach, trimming profits and limiting buybacks and dividends. This bill would have scrapped the rule outright and barred any substantially similar version, keeping the banks' existing lighter capital treatment in place while the public carries the downside risk through deposit insurance and bailout backstops [S2, S3].
